title: What to keep from Thoreau
hookLine: simplicity, wildness, conscience, attention to the small

cards: A suitcase, and not much room in it. That's roughly where this path is with Thoreau.
It has walked through a cabin, a bean field, a pond, a jail cell, a mountain, a shoreline, a journal and a sickroom, and tomorrow it leaves him. Nobody carries a whole writer out the door.
So today's question is a packing question: out of everything, what goes in the bag? Here are four things readers pick up from him. You only need one.

teach.b: First, simplicity. In Walden he writes, "Simplicity, simplicity, simplicity!" Three times, as if once weren't enough.
Fewer things, fewer affairs, so there's room left for a life. Second, wildness.
In Walking he writes, "In Wildness is the preservation of the World." Not wilderness only, out there: wildness, the part of the world, and of a person, that hasn't been tamed into usefulness.
It was there on Ktaadn, in his cry of contact. Third, conscience.

In his essay on civil government: "I think that we should be men first, and subjects afterward." A person before a citizen; conscience before convenience. That's the night in jail, folded into one sentence.
Fourth, attention to the small. No single slogan, because it's everywhere: the ice going out on the pond, the line in the journal, a violet's flowering, the stream he fishes in.
This week alone, he turned notebooks into seasons and time into water. And Emerson's teasing phrase fits too: the captain of a huckleberry party. Some might call that small.
It might be the whole point. Four doors into the same house. Some readers walk in through simplicity, some through the woods, some through protest, some through a notebook.
None is the right one. Thoreau wasn't tidy enough to be summed up in one, and his friends would remind you he wasn't easy either. But a person can carry one of these for years.

how: Some people who take something lasting from Thoreau settle on one thread, a simpler life, time in wild places, acts of conscience or close attention to nature, and build a small habit around it.

games.why: today's lesson: keep one. simplicity, wildness, conscience or attention to the small. one is enough.

practice: Let the four pass by slowly, one per breath: simplicity, wildness, conscience, attention to the small. Notice which one pulls at you, not the one you think you should choose, and let the other three go.
Ask what it might look like in an ordinary week: one thing given away, one walk in the rain, one honest no, one line in a notebook.

carryVoice: Your line: keep one. One door is enough to get into the house. I'll be here tomorrow.
